label: Problem set 11
title: Problem set 11: Bulk electrolysis
summary: Practice with Faradays law and coulometry: charge, number of electrons, amounts of substance, current efficiency and exhaustive electrolysis.

intro.text: Bulk electrolysis and coulometry apply Faradays law, Q = nF x moles. Measuring the charge passed gives the number of electrons, the amount of substance and the stoichiometry directly.
Controlled-potential electrolysis uses a chosen potential to be selective, and exhaustive electrolysis drives the reaction to completion as the current decays.

blocks.title: Charge for a deposition
blocks.given: mass = 100 mg Ag, n = 1, M(Ag) = 107.9 g/mol

questions.question: Calculate the charge in coulombs needed to deposit 100 mg of silver from Ag+ ions. Use n = 1, F = 96485 C/mol and the atomic mass of Ag = 107.9 g/mol.
A coulometric experiment passes 192.97 C and electrolyses exactly 1.00 mmol of a species. How many electrons per molecule are transferred? (n = Q/(F x moles).)
How long, in seconds, does it take to pass 89.4 C at a constant current of 0.100 A?
For a two-electron reaction, how many moles of substance are transformed by 1000 C? (N = Q/(nF).)
A deposition passes 100 C, but only 0.90 mmol of a one-electron product is obtained. Calculate the current efficiency as a fraction (charge useful/charge passed).
Faradays law of electrolysis states that the amount of substance transformed is:
questions.explanation: The amount transformed is proportional to the charge passed, with the constant of proportionality nF, so coulometry measures quantity of electricity directly.

questions.question: Controlled-potential bulk electrolysis can separate two species whose reduction potentials differ sufficiently.
questions.explanation: By holding the potential in a window where only one species reacts, that species is electrolysed selectively while the other is left largely untouched.

questions.question: Which quantities can be determined by coulometry (measuring total charge)? Select all that apply.
options: The number of electrons n in the reaction
questions.explanation: Coulometry gives n, the amount transformed and the stoichiometry, because charge is linked to moles by nF. Colour is not a coulometric quantity.

questions.question: In bulk electrolysis the goal is usually to convert the analyte exhaustively, so the current falls toward zero as it is consumed.
questions.explanation: As the analyte is depleted its bulk concentration falls, so the limiting current decays; the electrolysis is complete when essentially no reactant remains.

questions.question: If a bulk electrolysis uses 90 percent of the theoretical charge for the desired reaction, and the rest goes to a side reaction, what fraction of the current is wasted? (Answer as a fraction.)
questions.explanation: The fraction wasted is 1 - 0.90 = 0.10, i.e. 10 percent of the charge is lost to side reactions.

questions.question: Calculate the charge in coulombs needed to deposit 0.100 g of copper from Cu2+ (n = 2, M = 63.5 g/mol, F = 96485 C/mol).
How long, in seconds, does it take to pass 89.4 C at a constant current of 0.050 A?
The number of electrons n in a reaction is obtained coulometrically from:
questions.explanation: Measuring the charge Q for a known number of moles gives n = Q/(F x moles), provided the reaction is the only faradaic process occurring.

questions.question: A high current efficiency means most of the charge goes into the desired reaction rather than side reactions.
questions.explanation: Current efficiency is the fraction of the charge producing the desired product; side reactions lower it.

questions.question: Which conditions favour a clean, efficient bulk electrolysis? Select all that apply.
options: Good stirring to speed mass transport
A potential at the mass-transfer-limited plateau of the target species
Using the highest possible current with no control
questions.explanation: Stirring, a well-chosen potential and suppression of side reactions all improve an exhaustive electrolysis. Uncontrolled high current usually wastes charge on side reactions.
